design_detail: Echocardiography study in Brussels and Flanders, Belgium (December 2004 to February 2006): 29 people who had taken MDMA in the past year, recruited through the psychiatry departments of two general hospitals and help centres for people with drug problems, compared with 29 age- and sex-matched students who answered advertisements and reported no history of drug use (Am J Cardiol 2007;100:1442-1445; printed pp. 1442-1445, read as the published PDF). The paper calls itself case-control (p. 1445); because people were chosen by exposure and the outcome was measured once, the editors type it as a cross-sectional comparison. 33 people taking MDMA volunteered; 4 were excluded after scanning (3 for image quality, 1 for mitral and tricuspid prolapse), leaving 29 (p. 1443). Table 1 gives the demographics of the 33 and the echocardiographic results of the 29. Transthoracic echocardiograms of all four valves were stored, randomized and read blind by one of the sonographers and by an independent observer. 'Pathologic' follows the US Food and Drug Administration criteria for appetite-suppressant valve disease: mitral regurgitation of grade 2/4 or more, or aortic regurgitation of grade 1/4 or more. The laboratory mechanism (activation of the 5-HT2B receptor on human valve cells, Setola et al.) is cited, not tested.
can_establish: That in this recruited group a larger share of people who had taken MDMA in the past year (about six years of use on average, by their own account) had mild-to-moderate valve regurgitation, restrictive leaflet motion or strands on a blind-read echocardiogram than a matched group of drug-naive students: 8 of 29 (28%) met the FDA criteria against 0 of 29, and 13 of 29 had tricuspid regurgitation of grade 2/4 or more against 0 of 29.
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused the findings: there were no scans before use, the comparison group was students with no drug use at all, other drugs the MDMA group took are not reported, and the content of the tablets is unknown. How common valve changes are in people who take MDMA elsewhere (this group came through psychiatry and drug-help services). That the findings are harmful, since no symptoms, events or follow-up are reported. That the changes depend on the amount taken or are reversible: the dose comparison is within one small group and no repeat scans were done.

sample.recruitment: People who had taken MDMA in the past year were recruited by the psychiatry departments of two general hospitals and by help centres for people with drug problems in Brussels and Flanders; controls were age- and sex-matched students who answered advertisements and reported no drug use. All took part voluntarily with written consent (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 1442).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded in both groups: a history of ergot-derived drugs, Chinese herbs, appetite-suppressant drugs, intravenous drugs or any drug known to induce valve disease; any past cardiac disease (endocarditis, contractility abnormalities, hypertension); congenital or degenerative valve disease, including mitral or tricuspid prolapse, found on echocardiography; and poor image quality (p. 1442). Four of the 33 volunteers in the MDMA group were excluded after scanning (3 for image quality, 1 for mitral and tricuspid prolapse; Results, 1st paragraph, p. 1443).
sample.demographics: Table 1 (33 people taking MDMA, 29 controls): women 15 of 33 (45%) and 13 of 29 (45%); mean age 24.3 ± 3.1 and 25.6 ± 2.6 years (p = 0.10). MDMA use in the 33: 3.6 ± 6.7 tablets a week for 6.1 ± 3.4 years; all had used for at least 6 months (p. 1443).
sample.attrition: 4 of 33 people in the MDMA group (12%) were excluded after scanning; no exclusions after enrolment are reported for the controls (p. 1443).
sample.selection_effects: The exposed people came from psychiatry departments and drug-help centres and the controls from student advertisements, matched only on age and sex, so differences in other drug use, tobacco, alcohol, medicines and the reasons for seeking care are built into the comparison. The weekly tablet figure (3.6 ± 6.7) has a spread nearly twice its mean, which suggests a skewed distribution with a few much higher values. The authors call the sample small because people were hard to recruit (p. 1445). Exclusions after scanning were reported only for the MDMA group.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported MDMA use in a detailed interview by an experienced psychiatrist about current and past drug use (p. 1442); no biological test, no analysis of tablets. Reported as tablets a week, years of use and, in the text, cumulative tablets (p. 1444).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: 3.6 ± 6.7 tablets a week for 6.1 ± 3.4 years in the 33 people recruited (Table 1); on average 943 ± 1,162 cumulative tablets in those with higher grades of regurgitation and 242 ± 212 in those with lower grades (p. 1444). These are descriptions of the group studied, not amounts to take.
exposure.polysubstance: The psychiatrist asked about other drugs because substance use is mostly not limited to one drug (p. 1442), but the paper reports nothing about what else the MDMA group took or how it was handled; the comparison is with people reporting no drug use at all. Use of drugs known to induce valve disease was an exclusion criterion.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported. The abstract says 'using or having used' MDMA, the Methods say use in the past year; time since last use is not given.

comparison.controls: 29 students who answered advertisements, matched for age and sex, with no history of drug use and the same exclusion criteria (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 1442).
comparison.matching: Age and sex. Table 1: women 45% in both groups; age 24.3 ± 3.1 against 25.6 ± 2.6 years, p = 0.10 (editors' note: a standardised difference of about 0.45 for 33 against 29, so close but not equal).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No scans before use (the authors: 'There were no echocardiographic data available before MDMA use'). Not reported or adjusted: other drug use, tobacco, alcohol, blood pressure, body size, psychiatric diagnoses and any medicines taken for them.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls reported no drug use of any kind. The other drug use of the MDMA group was asked about but is not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Transthoracic echocardiography (GE Vivid 7), all four valves from all possible views; continuous-wave, pulse-wave and colour Doppler; regurgitation graded 1 to 4 by American Society of Echocardiography recommendations; regurgitant jet-to-atrium area ratio for the mitral and tricuspid valves. Images stored digitally, randomized and read blind by one of the sonographers and an independent observer (Methods, p. 1443).
outcomes.validity_norms: FDA criteria were written for appetite-suppressant valve disease (mitral regurgitation 2/4 or more, aortic regurgitation 1/4 or more). The authors note that trace or mild mitral and tricuspid regurgitation is common in the general population (p. 1443). Interobserver agreement on the FDA score: kappa above 0.9 (Results, p. 1443). The authors say the scoring system of their earlier pergolide study was built for an older population (p. 1444).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Pathologic' = FDA criteria (mitral 2/4 or more, or aortic 1/4 or more). Other outcomes: tricuspid regurgitation 2/4 or more, pulmonary regurgitation 1/4 or more, area ratios, restrictive leaflet motion (leaflets stiffer than normal, tips closing towards the apex) and 'strands' (thin, mobile, filamentous projections on the leaflets). No symptoms, pressures, events or follow-up are reported.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; every test two-tailed at p of 0.05 or less (p. 1443). Editors' count of 12 outcomes: the 10 echocardiographic rows of Table 1, the composite FDA criterion and the combined strand count in the abstract; the within-group cumulative-dose comparison and the demographic tests are not counted. By the paper's rule 7 of the 12 reach p of 0.05 or less.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Reading was blind to group (randomized images, two readers, kappa above 0.9). The sonographers who acquired the images are described as not informed of the patients' identities; whether they knew a person's group is not stated (p. 1442).

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 1 (29 people taking MDMA against 29 controls; percentages and intervals added by the editors from the printed counts, Wilson 95% intervals; the paper's Fisher exact p values were reproduced from the counts). FDA criteria 8/29 (28%, 15-46%) against 0/29 (upper 95% bound about 12%), p = 0.0045. Tricuspid regurgitation 2/4 or more 13/29 (45%, 28-62%) against 0, p < 0.001; tricuspid area ratio 19 ± 9.5% against 9 ± 4.5%, p < 0.001. Mitral regurgitation 2/4 or more 4/29 (14%, 5-31%) against 0, p = 0.11; mitral area ratio 12 ± 9.8% against 5 ± 1.3%, p < 0.007; mitral restrictive motion 7/29 (24%, 12-42%) against 0, p = 0.01. Aortic regurgitation 1/4 or more 4/29 (14%) against 0, p = 0.11. Strands: mitral 1/29, aortic 5/29 and combined 6/29 (21%, 10-38%) against 0, p = 0.02 for the combined count. Tricuspid restrictive motion 5/29 against 1/29, p = 0.19; pulmonary regurgitation 1/4 or more 14/29 (48%) against 10/29 (34%), p = 0.42. Within the MDMA group, people with higher grades of regurgitation had taken on average 943 ± 1,162 cumulative tablets against 242 ± 212 in those with lower grades, p = 0.03 (p. 1444).
analysis.covariates: None for the valve outcomes: groups matched on age and sex only. Relative risks with 95% intervals are described as from logistic regression (p. 1443) but the paper does not say what was adjusted for; the printed 5.83 for tricuspid restrictive motion equals the crude odds ratio from the counts (editors' calculation).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol mentioned; ethics committee approval only (p. 1442).
analysis.selective_reporting: No primary outcome is named. The abstract reports mitral regurgitation of 1/4 in 6 people (p = 0.002) and combined strands (p = 0.02), neither of which has a row in Table 1; the abstract's mitral area-ratio p of 0.007 is printed '<0.007' in Table 1.
analysis.power: No power calculation; 29 per group. The authors say the size is relatively small because people were hard to recruit (p. 1445).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 29 people who had taken MDMA (recruited through psychiatry and drug-help services) 8 (28%) had valve findings meeting the FDA criteria against none of 29 matched drug-naive students. The largest differences were tricuspid regurgitation of grade 2/4 or more (13 of 29 against 0) and the regurgitant area ratios, with mitral restrictive motion in 7 against 0 and strands in 6 against 0; mitral and aortic regurgitation at the FDA thresholds were found in 4 of 29 each against 0 (p = 0.11 each, not significant on its own). Pulmonary regurgitation was common in both groups (14 of 29 and 10 of 29, p = 0.42). Regurgitation was mostly mild to moderate; no symptoms or outcomes are reported. Within the MDMA group, people with higher grades had taken more tablets in total on average (943 against 242, with a wide spread).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title says 'possible association', but the abstract concludes that 'MDMA may lead to mild to moderate valvular heart disease and valvular strands'; the Discussion says severity was associated with cumulative dose ('dose-dependent'), that lesions weaker than with pergolide or fenfluramine-phentermine could be explained by reversibility between weekends of use, that the findings are 'of great clinical importance' and that they argue for endocarditis prophylaxis (pp. 1444-1445). The comparison with drug-naive students, the absence of pre-use scans and unreported other drug use leave the group difference unattributed; the dose comparison is within one small group and cannot separate amount from years of use; reversibility was not tested; no clinical outcome or symptom is reported.

timeline.event: Laboratory study: MDMA and its metabolite activate human 5-HT2B receptors and drive prolonged growth of human valve cells in a dish (Setola et al.; cited in this paper, not tested).
Same group's earlier study of restrictive valve disease with pergolide in Parkinson's disease (Van Camp et al., Lancet; cited in this paper).
This paper: the authors state it is the first report of valve disease in young adults using or having used MDMA (Discussion, p. 1444).

replication.where_it_stands: The paper presents itself as the first report and cites no replication. This card does not review later studies, so the status reflects only what the paper reports and should be checked against later echocardiography work before a claim is published.

funding.funder: The first author received a scholarship from the Fonds voor Wetenschappelijk Onderzoek Vlaanderen (Brussels) for this work; no other funding is stated (p. 1442).
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated: the paper has no conflict-of-interest statement. A statistician is thanked for advice (p. 1445).
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of cardiology and psychiatry at two Brussels hospitals (Universitair Ziekenhuis Brussel; CHU St. Pieter). Several authors had earlier reported restrictive valve disease with pergolide in Parkinson's disease (Van Camp et al., 2004), and the paper uses that experience to frame the MDMA findings.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study that scans people before they start MDMA, or follows a representative group of people taking it, with repeat blind echocardiograms, a comparison group from the same community checked for other drugs and medicines, confirmed content of what was taken, symptoms and clinical outcomes recorded, and repeat scans after people stop to test reversibility.

domains.note: Matched on age and sex only; controls were students with no drug use, the MDMA group came through psychiatry and drug-help services; other drugs, tobacco, alcohol, medicines and psychiatric diagnoses are not reported or adjusted for.
Self-report in an interview, no biological test, tablet content unknown, cumulative tablets reported with a spread larger than the mean (943 ± 1,162).
Exposed people from psychiatry departments and drug-help centres against advertised student controls; 4 of 33 exposed people were excluded after scanning and only for the MDMA group.
4 of 33 (12%) of the MDMA group were left out of the echocardiographic analysis; Table 1 gives the demographics and MDMA use for the 33 and the echocardiographic results for the 29.
Randomized images read blind by two readers with kappa above 0.9 and standard criteria; restrictive motion and strands are the authors' own definitions.
No primary outcome; 12 outcomes without correction; two abstract results (mitral 1/4 and combined strands) have no row in Table 1; printed relative risks are not reproducible from the counts.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The outcome measurement is the strongest part (blind, independent reader, standard criteria), but the comparison cannot separate MDMA from the other differences between a group recruited through psychiatric and drug-help services and drug-naive students, from other drugs taken, or from the unknown content of the tablets, and there were no scans before use. The study may be cited for a difference in echocardiographic findings between these two recruited groups; it may not be cited for MDMA causing valve disease, for how common it is, for dose dependence or for reversibility.

key_findings.finding: Abstract: 29 people using or having used MDMA and 29 gender- and age-matched controls were evaluated blind by echocardiography. 8 (28%) of the MDMA group met FDA criteria for appetite-suppressant valve disease against none of the controls (p = 0.0045); mitral regurgitation of 1/4 in 6 (21%) and over 2/4 in 4 (14%) against none (p = 0.002); mean mitral area ratios 12 ± 9.8% against 5 ± 1.3% (p = 0.007); tricuspid regurgitation over 2/4 in 13 (45%) against none (p < 0.001), area ratios 19 ± 9.5% against 9 ± 4.5%; mild aortic regurgitation in 4 (14%, p = 0.11); strands in 6 (21%) against none (p = 0.02). Conclusion: 'MDMA may lead to mild to moderate valvular heart disease and valvular strands'.
key_findings.note: The abstract says 'over 2/4'; Table 1 and the Methods use 2/4 or more.

key_findings.finding: Recruitment and criteria: people who had taken MDMA in the past year came from the psychiatry departments of two general hospitals and from help centres for people with drug problems in Brussels and Flanders (December 2004 to February 2006); controls were age- and sex-matched students who answered advertisements and reported no drug use. A psychiatrist interviewed everyone about current and past drug use. Exclusions in both groups: ergot-derived drugs, Chinese herbs, appetite suppressants, intravenous drugs or other drugs known to induce valve disease; any cardiac disease; congenital or degenerative valve disease on echocardiography; poor images.

Echocardiography and analysis: all images were stored, randomized and read blind by one of the sonographers and an independent observer; mitral and tricuspid regurgitant area ratio was also calculated. The FDA criteria were used (mitral regurgitation 2/4 or more, aortic regurgitation 1/4 or more) because trace or mild regurgitation of the mitral and tricuspid valves is common in the general population. Fisher exact, chi-square, Student t and Mann-Whitney tests; relative risks from logistic regression; two-tailed, p of 0.05 or less significant; SPSS 14.

Participants and headline result: 33 people who took MDMA and 29 controls were selected; none had a history of cardiac disease; 4 in the MDMA group were excluded (3 for image quality, 1 for mitral and tricuspid prolapse). Demographics were the same in the two groups; kappa between the two blinded observers was above 0.9; all people in the MDMA group had used for at least 6 months. Eight (28%) of the MDMA group had pathologic results by the FDA criteria and none of the controls (p = 0.0045).

Table 1, demographics (controls against MDMA group): n 29 and 33; women 13 (45%) and 15 (45%); age 25.6 ± 2.6 and 24.3 ± 3.1 years (p = 0.10); MDMA dose 3.6 ± 6.7 tablets a week; duration 6.1 ± 3.4 years.
key_findings.note: Demographics are for the 33 recruited, the echocardiographic rows for the 29 analysed.

key_findings.finding: Table 1, echocardiography (n = 29 each; controls against MDMA group): mitral regurgitation 2/4 or more 0 and 4 (14%), p = 0.11; mitral area ratio 5 ± 1.3% and 12 ± 9.8%, p < 0.007; mitral restrictive motion 0 and 7 (24%), p = 0.01; mitral strand 0 and 1 (3%), p > 0.99; aortic regurgitation 1/4 or more 0 and 4 (14%), p = 0.11; aortic strand 0 and 5 (17%), p = 0.05; tricuspid regurgitation 2/4 or more 0 and 13 (45%), p < 0.001; tricuspid area ratio 9 ± 4.5% and 19 ± 9.5%, p < 0.001; tricuspid restrictive motion 1 (3%) and 5 (17%), p = 0.19; pulmonary regurgitation 1/4 or more 10 (34%) and 14 (48%), p = 0.42.
key_findings.note: Editors recalculated Fisher exact p values from the counts and reproduced the printed ones (for example 0.0045, 0.11, 0.01, 0.19, 0.42, 0.02 for the combined strands).

key_findings.finding: Within the MDMA group, people with regurgitation of 2/4 or more on the mitral or tricuspid valves or any aortic regurgitation had on average taken more cumulative tablets (943 ± 1,162) than those with lower grades (242 ± 212; p = 0.03). The lesions were restrictive leaflet lesions at the mitral and tricuspid valves, regurgitation and strands. The authors cite laboratory work (Setola et al.) showing that MDMA and its metabolite activate human 5-HT2B receptors and induce prolonged growth responses in human valve cells, and conclude that severity was associated with cumulative dose.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Group sizes within the MDMA group and the method of calculating cumulative tablets are not given.

key_findings.finding: Interpretation: the authors report valve disease for the first time in young adults using or having used MDMA; they explain the milder lesions compared with pergolide or fenfluramine-phentermine by possible reversibility between weekends of use, state that the regurgitations could become more severe with increasing doses and duration, and call the findings 'of great clinical importance', adding that endocarditis prophylaxis should be argued for.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th to 6th paragraphs (the 5th, beginning 'The party drug MDMA is more frequently used', runs from p. 1444 to p. 1445; the 6th begins on p. 1445)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated: MDMA is illegal, so people were hard to recruit and the size is relatively small; information on the quantity of use came from interviews; there were no echocardiographic data before MDMA use because prospective evaluation was not possible in this case-control study for ethical reasons; there is no pathological evidence because no valve surgery was needed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (beginning 'This study has some limitations')

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 reports the demographics and MDMA use (3.6 ± 6.7 tablets a week, 6.1 ± 3.4 years) for 33 people but the echocardiographic results for 29; the 4 people excluded after scanning are included in the first and not the second.
reporting_issues.consequence: The exposure description does not strictly describe the people whose valves were analysed.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives mitral and tricuspid regurgitation as 'over 2/4' (4 and 13 people), but the Methods and Table 1 define the criterion as 2/4 or more. The abstract's 'mitral regurgitation of 1/4 in 6 (21%)' and its p of 0.002 have no row in Table 1; the abstract's combined strands (6, p = 0.02) are also not a Table 1 row (mitral 1 and aortic 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Two of the abstract's headline results cannot be traced to the table; the counts can be checked only through the text.

reporting_issues.issue: The mitral area ratio is given as p = 0.007 in the abstract and '<0.007' in Table 1, next to a relative risk of 1.68 whose 95% interval (0.99-2.84) includes 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed p and interval for the same variable point in different directions; the relative risk for a continuous ratio is not explained.

reporting_issues.issue: The relative risks are said to come from logistic regression, but the paper does not say what was adjusted for. The printed 5.83 for tricuspid restrictive motion equals the crude odds ratio from the counts (5 of 29 against 1 of 29), and the printed 1.34 for pulmonary regurgitation matches neither the crude risk ratio (1.40) nor the odds ratio (1.77); relative risks are also printed for sex (0.99) and age (0.85) without units.
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed 'relative risks' cannot be interpreted as risk ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: Cumulative tablets are given only as two subgroup means (943 ± 1,162 and 242 ± 212) with no subgroup sizes, ranges or method of calculation; if 3.6 tablets a week applied to every week of 6.1 years it would come to about 1,100 tablets, above both subgroup means, so the figures may not describe the same people or the same weeks of use (the four excluded people may also differ).
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose comparison cannot be checked or reproduced; its spread (standard deviation above the mean) means a few people carry the difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper calls the design case-control (limitations), but people were chosen by exposure and the valves measured once, not selected by outcome.
reporting_issues.consequence: The design label suggests a stronger inference than a one-time comparison of two recruited groups supports.

reporting_issues.issue: The strength of the claim rises through the paper: the title says 'possible association', the abstract 'may lead to', and the Discussion 'dose-dependent relation' and findings 'of great clinical importance', with a recommendation about endocarditis prophylaxis that no data in the paper test.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the results and the limitations, not the Discussion's causal and clinical statements.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1442-1445 (PDFs/MDMA/Droogmans_2007_ValvularHeartDisease.pdf), full text including the reference list; extracted once with pdftotext, which garbled symbols; Table 1 (p. 1443) and the abstract symbols were checked against 110 dpi renderings, and the paper's Fisher exact p values were recomputed from the counts.
